cards.title: Designing more efficient quantum circuits with Claude

depth.text: Claude found ways to make **eight quantum circuits** use **fewer qubits and gates**

Across eight computational tasks, Claude proposed circuits, got correctness checks and cost scores from an evaluator, then revised its designs. For elliptic-curve point addition, one design used **12% more qubits** but **17x fewer gates** than the smallest previous design. A separate decoder redesign cut gate count by a factor of 12 compared with Google’s previous construction.

gates vs. smallest previous point-addition design

That means LLMs benefit from the closed loop of verification, and can rapidly test and discard ideas. It's not too surprising that previous academics…

cards.title: What on Earth Is Dekton?

depth.text: someone explains how **Dekton** is **basically porcelain**, but made tougher for kitchen surfaces

Cosentino invented it in 2013; it’s made from ground porcelain, glass and quartz, then pressed with **25,000 metric tons** of force and hardened at **1,200 degrees centigrade**. Making it took **six years and almost $200 million**, and the process nearly removes porcelain’s usual brittleness.

cards.camps: Two camps: some commenters say Dekton shrugs off heat, spills and scratches; others say focused impacts can make it shatter.

comments.text: It’s interesting that the focus is on porcelain as a cooking surface but misses the biggest reasons for it displacing engineered quartz or granite for countertops. There’s a few factors at play here leading to the prominence of porcelain. For the induction cooktops, you can cut porcelain slabs to 6mm compared to your 3cm (sometimes 2cm) quartz and granite. This is also why you can use it for…

I wanted Dekton for my new countertops. Its list of resistances to various kitchen mishaps was extremely impressive. Every other material we looked at has at least one weakness. Dekton was marketed as having none. It also looked quite good, being available in lots of colors and patterns. The real drawback was going to be the price. It's basically the most expensive countertop material (or was, 2…

The article misses an important bit of context (imo) that low thermal expansion glasses like CERAN have been around for ages and anyone who’s used an induction or a glass top stove would be familiar. However you can now get completely hidden stoves that look like stone countertops. If you’re not in the market for a kitchen, or know anyone people who recently remodeled it’s reasonable to not know…

Had a new kitchen and bathroom installed last year. Most surfaces (kitchen counter, shower and general bath room) all Dekton or one of Cosentino’s other lines. I was apprehensive: it is expensive and “not real stone”. Super happy with it. Spilling red wine, putting sizzling hot pans on it, accidentally dropping big pans on it. Dekton brushes it off. Go into debt if you have to.
We're getting a new kitchen and this is all my wife is talking about. Good help me.

cards.title: Solar surpasses nuclear power globally for first time – pv magazine Global

depth.text: **solar** generated **more electricity than nuclear** globally for the first time, with wind also gaining ground

The report says monthly solar generation passed nuclear in **April 2025**, then beat it for the year as solar output grew **30%** and nuclear output rose 1.1%. Newer IEA PVPS data put 2025 global PV additions at **around 690 GW**, about 180 GW above the report’s figure.

cards.camps: Two camps: solar boosters celebrate its rise; nuclear supporters say nuclear is still worth building and solar has limits.

comments.text: It is a shame that nuclear power has stagnated - we could have been moving towards fossil fuel free grid half a century ago. We've lost decades of progress there. But it's a good thing that solar power is coming into its own more and more. Late is better than never.

By comparison, installed nuclear…

Note that this is actual generated terawatt hours. Nuclear power has a substantially higher capacity factor, but solar has been growing so rapidly that it has taken the lead on generated output too. Wind is just about to surpass nuclear generation also, though solar is racing ahead much faster. The next big milestone, not to be reached for several years at the present rate, would be solar…

Always good to see the future arriving, but the job is not done yet by far. We need to be sure not to take our foot off the gas (figuratively of course). We need to accelerate clean energy generation even more so we can replace not just dirty electricity sources but dirty energy sources entirely, and produce synthetic petrochemical feedstocks. Modernity runs on hydrocarbons-as-chemicals, not just…

On a monthly basis. News articles about solar power tend to quote maximum capacity, confusing the issue. This is about energy rather than power, aggregated over a month, so it's a somewhat more meaningful statement.

cards.title: How the Claude Code team does code review

depth.text: the Claude Code team lets **machines** handle most review and saves people for **risky decisions**

Every pull request gets a **Claude review** before a person looks. Human review changes with the **risk**: a docs fix and an auto-updater change get different treatment. From June to September, merged pull requests more than doubled while the share that had to be reverted fell by **more than 40 percent**.

cards.title: You could have invented transformers from memory

depth.text: someone shows how you could **build up transformers** by treating each layer as a **memory store**

It starts with an **outer-product store**, treats MLPs as memory stores, then explains **self-attention** as a store whose keys and values come from context tokens. For random keys and values, it estimates **about 1.2 million memories** when querying a stored key at β = √d_k = 8; scaling β with log M lets distinct-key capacity grow essentially without bound.

cards.camps: Two camps: some praise the article's accessible math; others say the notation and lack of a concrete example make it hard to follow.

cards.title: Big Fish: Exploiting a 37-Year-Old Kernel Bug in OpenBSD

depth.text: someone exploited a 37-year-old **OpenBSD bug** to get a **root shell**

A shared-memory attachment counter was a signed 16-bit short; repeated process forks could push it past **32,767** and make it wrap negative. Combined with a separate **out-of-bounds write** in the kernel, that enabled local privilege escalation to **root**; the issues were addressed in errata 026 and 018.

cards.camps: Two camps: some praised the graphics; others found the AI-generated graphic a turnoff.

comments.text: Props for the OpenBSD Release -style graphics. Looking forward to the theme song.
Interestingly, looks like this was accidentally fixed in NetBSD during a rewrite of that code in August of 1999.

It’s remarkable that a bug survived 37 years in one of the most heavily audited codebases, which shows how hard some kernel bugs are to catch by review alone. Do you think fuzzing or static analysis could realistically have found this class of bug, or did it need a human thinking about the exploit primitive?

Poor OpenBSD guys. Now they have to acknowledge THREE exploits
(in total) on their homepage.

glossary.local LLM: Large language model: an AI that works with text; a local one runs on your own device.
glossary.benchmark: A test people use to compare how well different tools do a task.
glossary.quantization: A way to make a model use less computing power by representing its internal numbers less precisely.
glossary.context window: The amount of text and information an AI can take into account at one time.
glossary.KV cache: A store of earlier model calculations that it can reuse instead of doing them again.
glossary.VRAM: The memory inside a graphics card that holds information the AI needs while running.
glossary.quantum circuit: A sequence of operations that tells a quantum computer how to calculate.
glossary.qubit: A unit of quantum information, described here as a possible basic ingredient of reality.
glossary.gate: A basic operation that a quantum computer applies to qubits during a calculation.
glossary.superposition: When a network uses the same internal parts to represent several different things, making them harder to tell apart.
glossary.modular inversion: Division with numbers that wrap back around at a fixed limit.
glossary.divsteps: A method that repeatedly simplifies a pair of numbers to find a modular inverse.
glossary.syndrome: A compact summary of errors that helps a decoder work out where they occurred.
glossary.decoder: A program that uses a summary of errors to find where they occurred and what they were.
glossary.materials science: The study of how a material’s makeup affects its physical properties.
glossary.kaolin: A soft, pale clay used in making porcelain.
glossary.kaolinite: A mineral found in kaolin clay.
glossary.hydraulic press: A machine that uses liquid pressure to squeeze something with great force.
glossary.silicosis: A lung disease caused by breathing in silica dust.
glossary.thermal shock: Damage caused when a material experiences a sudden temperature change.
glossary.PV: Photovoltaic: solar panels that turn sunlight into electricity.

glossary.TWh: Terawatt-hour: a way to count a huge amount of electricity produced or used.
glossary.SMRs: Small modular reactors: smaller nuclear plant designs meant to be built in sections.
glossary.BESS: Battery energy storage system: equipment that saves electricity so it can be used later.
glossary.capacity factor: How much electricity a plant makes over time compared with what it could make if it ran at full output.
glossary.agentic model: An AI that can take steps toward completing a task, rather than only replying to a prompt.
glossary.reinforcement learning: A way to train an AI by rewarding choices that work and discouraging choices that do not.
glossary.base model: The starting AI that someone builds on or adapts for a particular use.
glossary.context injection: Adding extra information or instructions to what an AI sees before it responds.
glossary.harness: The surrounding code that gives an AI agent tools and a place to work, and checks what it does.
glossary.guardrails: Instructions that tell an AI how it should respond.
glossary.Butlerian Jihad: In Dune, the fight against thinking machines and the people in charge of them.
glossary.technocrats: People who use their technical expertise or control of technology to hold political power.
glossary.plot armor: A story setup that lets events happen even when they seem like they should be stopped.
glossary.AI: Artificial intelligence: computer systems designed to do tasks people associate with thinking.
glossary.LLMs: Large language models: computer programs trained on lots of writing that can produce text.
glossary.probabilistic: Able to give different results because chance is involved.
glossary.deterministic: Something that gives the same result when it gets the same input.
glossary.agentic tasks: Work where an AI can take steps toward a goal, not just answer a question.
glossary.chat template: A set of rules for laying out a conversation so the model can read each message correctly.
glossary.open weights: The model's learned settings are available for people to download and run themselves.
glossary.text-to-image: Making a picture from a written description.
glossary.multi-reference generation: Making a new picture while using several supplied images as examples.
glossary.INT8: A compact way to store a model's numbers that can reduce the memory needed to run it.
glossary.step distilled model: A version set up to make an image in fewer steps, which can make generation faster.
glossary.sparse mixture-of-experts: A model with many specialized parts that only uses some of them for each request.
glossary.Causal Encoder-Decoder (CED): Causal Encoder-Decoder: the name for a design that describes how an AI takes in information and produces an answer.
glossary.KV caching: A way to keep useful pieces of earlier text ready, so the model does less repeated work.

glossary.revert: Undo a code change, usually after it causes a problem.
glossary.feature flag: A switch developers can use to turn a feature on or off without removing it from the program.
glossary.merge queue: A waiting line that checks code changes before adding them to the shared project.
glossary.CI: Continuous integration: automatic checks that run when developers change code, helping catch problems early.
glossary.GGUF: GPT-Generated Unified Format: a file type for saving an AI model so compatible programs can use it.
glossary.GPU: Graphics Processing Unit: the chip part that draws images and video.
glossary.jailbroken: Modified to let a device run software its maker normally restricts.
glossary.firmware: The built-in software that tells a device's hardware how to work.

glossary.RF: Radio frequency: radio waves used to carry signals through the air.
glossary.transformer: A kind of language model that can weigh how different words in a passage relate to each other.
glossary.outer-product memory store: A simple store that combines a key and its value in a table so later inputs can look up the information.
glossary.MLP: Multi-layer perceptron: a part of the model that processes information through several linked steps.
glossary.self-attention: A way for an AI to work out which other parts of the text matter most to each part it is reading.
glossary.key-value pair: A pair where a key helps find the information attached to it, like a label and what it points to.
glossary.softmax: A calculation that turns a set of scores into weights that add up to one.

glossary.shared memory: A part of a computer's memory that multiple running programs can use to share information.
glossary.integer overflow: When a number gets bigger than its storage allows and wraps around to a different value.
glossary.use-after-free: Trying to use data after it has been discarded.
glossary.local privilege escalation: A way for someone already on a computer to gain more control, such as administrator access.
glossary.root shell: A place to type commands with the highest level of control over a computer.
glossary.ECI: Economic Complexity Index: a score the article uses to compare how complex different economies are.
glossary.Spearman rank correlation: A way to check whether two groups of things tend to appear in a similar order.
